question: What is the primary goal of the living will movement?

options.A: To give doctors full authority over end-of-life care
options.B: To speed up the legal probate process for families
options.C: To help patients control their medical treatment choices ahead of time
options.D: To reduce overall hospital costs for elderly patients

explanation: The entire movement centers on letting individuals make their treatment preferences known before they lose the ability to speak for themselves. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h1)

question: Why is the living will movement considered a shift away from medical paternalism?

options.A: Because nurses take over the legal responsibilities of physicians
options.B: Because patients now direct their care instead of doctors making every choice
options.C: Because hospitals no longer require doctors to write treatment orders
options.D: Because family members now pay all medical bills directly

explanation: Traditional medical paternalism meant doctors decided everything. Living wills put the decision-making power back into the hands of the patient. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h1)

question: Which federal law requires healthcare facilities to inform patients about advance directives upon admission?
explanation: Passed in 1991, the Patient Self-Determination Act ensures that patients are told about their right to make advance directives when entering a healthcare facility. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h2)

question: What was a major legal outcome of the Nancy Cruzan case regarding end-of-life care?

options.A: It established the need for clear evidence of a patient's prior treatment wishes
options.B: It created the very first living will document in history
options.C: It gave physicians the final say in removing feeding tubes
options.D: It banned families from ever stopping life support

explanation: The Supreme Court ruled that states could require clear and convincing evidence of what the patient would have wanted before stopping life support. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h2)

question: What is the main role of a healthcare proxy or durable power of attorney?

options.A: To pay the patient's medical bills out of their personal bank account
options.B: To write the medical orders that the doctor must follow
options.C: To provide nursing care inside the patient's home
options.D: To make medical decisions when the patient loses capacity

explanation: A healthcare proxy is a designated person who speaks for the patient and makes treatment choices when the patient can no longer do so. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h3)

question: A patient is unconscious and has a living will that lists specific rejected treatments, but a brand-new medical complication arises that is not mentioned in the paper. What is the main limitation of relying solely on the living will here?

options.A: Living wills automatically expire after five years in the hospital
options.B: Living wills can be too rigid to cover every unexpected clinical situation
options.C: Living wills only apply to surgical procedures, not medical treatments
options.D: Living wills must be approved by a judge before nurses can read them

explanation: Because a living will is a written list, it cannot anticipate every medical scenario, which is why having a healthcare proxy is also valuable. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h3)

question: Which ethical principle directly supports a competent patient's right to refuse medical treatment?
explanation: Autonomy is the ethical principle that respects an individual's right to make independent choices about their own body and healthcare. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h4)

question: Why might a nurse experience ethical conflict when carrying out a patient's request to stop life support?

options.A: Fearing that the hospital will refuse to pay the nurse's salary
options.B: Believing that living wills have no legal standing in a hospital
options.C: Balancing the duty to do no harm with the duty to respect patient choices
options.D: Knowing that doctors are legally required to ignore advance directives

explanation: Nurses want to protect life, so stopping life support can feel emotionally difficult even though respecting the patient's autonomy is legally and ethically correct. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h4)

question: What is a common misconception about advance care planning in healthcare?

options.A: That patients must pay a fee to create an advance directive
options.B: That doctors must approve every sentence written in a living will
options.C: That it is just a one-time signature on a legal form rather than an ongoing conversation
options.D: That nurses are legally forbidden from talking about living wills

explanation: Advance care planning is a continuous process of communication between patients, families, and providers, not just paperwork. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h5)

question: Why is discussing the realities of life support important during advance care planning?

options.A: It reduces the amount of paperwork nurses must file in the chart
options.B: It prevents family members from ever disagreeing with the doctor
options.C: It helps patients give truly informed consent for what they want or reject
options.D: It guarantees that the patient will live longer in the hospital

explanation: Patients need to know what procedures like CPR or ventilation actually involve so their choices are genuinely informed. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common barrier to using living wills in clinical practice?

options.A: Vaguely written instructions like 'no heroic measures'
options.B: Having too many copies of the document easily available to doctors
options.C: Family members disputing the wishes during an emergency
options.D: Documents being left at home instead of brought to the hospital

explanation: Having too many accessible copies is rarely a problem; the usual issue is that documents are hidden at home or poorly written. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h6)

question: Why do vaguely worded living wills cause problems for the healthcare team?

options.A: Because nurses are not legally allowed to read handwritten documents
options.B: Because insurance companies refuse to pay for vague medical forms
options.C: Because hospitals require notarized stamps on every single page
options.D: Because terms like 'heroic measures' can mean different things to different people

explanation: Vague phrases create ambiguity, leaving nurses and physicians unsure of whether the patient intended to refuse specific interventions like intubation or IV fluids. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h6)

question: What is a primary nursing responsibility regarding advance directives upon patient admission?

options.A: Deciding whether the living will is legally valid without a doctor
options.B: Writing the legal documents for the patient using hospital letterhead
options.C: Notifying the local court system that a new patient has arrived
options.D: Asking about existing directives and placing copies in the medical record

explanation: Nurses routinely screen for advance directives upon admission to ensure the care team knows the patient's preferences from the start. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h7)

question: An adult child is crying and demanding that staff restart all life support for a dying parent, even though the parent has a clear living will stating otherwise. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Act as an advocate for the patient by gently reminding the family of the documented wishes
options.B: Tell the family that their opinion does not matter at all in the hospital
options.C: Immediately follow the child's orders to stop the family conflict
options.D: Call hospital security to remove the family member from the room

explanation: The nurse bridges the gap with compassion, offering emotional support while firmly upholding the documented autonomy of the patient. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h7)
